source: A Classical Introduction to Modern Number Theory -- Kenneth Ireland, Michael Rosen -.pdf; rewritten seed rule
name: Chord-and-tangent addition law
statement: On a nonsingular plane cubic with a chosen point at infinity, the third intersection point of a line defines addition of rational points after reflection.
conditions: E is a nonsingular elliptic curve in Weierstrass form over a field of characteristic not causing singular formulas.
P and Q are points on E over the field.
conclusion: The chord-and-tangent construction gives a point P+Q on E over the same field and makes E a group with identity O.
typical_uses: Check algebraic manipulations involving sums of rational points.
common_misuses: Using nonsingular group-law formulas on a singular cubic or at vertical-line cases without special handling.
bridge_lemmas: A line intersects a cubic in three points counted with multiplicity.
repair_templates: Verify the discriminant is nonzero and handle P=Q or Q=-P using the tangent or point-at-infinity cases.

source: A Classical Introduction to Modern Number Theory -- Kenneth Ireland, Michael Rosen -.pdf; rewritten seed rule
name: Weak Mordell-Weil for 2-descent
statement: For an elliptic curve over Q, the quotient of rational points by twice rational points is finite.
conditions: E is an elliptic curve defined over Q.
conclusion: E(Q)/2E(Q) is a finite group.
typical_uses: Start a height descent proving finite generation of E(Q).
common_misuses: Confusing finiteness of E(Q)/2E(Q) with finiteness of E(Q).
bridge_lemmas: The descent map lands in a finite subgroup controlled by finitely many ideals or square classes.
repair_templates: Use weak Mordell-Weil together with a height reduction argument before concluding finite generation.

source: A Classical Introduction to Modern Number Theory -- Kenneth Ireland, Michael Rosen -.pdf; rewritten seed rule
name: Bounded height finiteness
statement: Only finitely many rational or algebraic points have bounded height over a fixed number field and bounded degree data.
conditions: K is a fixed number field or Q in the rational case.
A height bound C is fixed.
Points or algebraic numbers are restricted to the given field.
conclusion: There are finitely many objects in K with height at most C.
typical_uses: Complete descent proofs by ruling out infinitely many strictly decreasing or bounded-height exceptions.
common_misuses: Using bounded height finiteness while allowing the field degree to vary without bound.
bridge_lemmas: Height bounds control numerator and denominator sizes in fixed degree.
repair_templates: Fix the base field and degree before invoking finiteness of bounded height.

source: A Classical Introduction to Modern Number Theory -- Kenneth Ireland, Michael Rosen -.pdf; rewritten seed rule
name: Faltings theorem for curves of genus greater than one
statement: A smooth projective curve of genus greater than one over a number field has only finitely many rational points over that field.
conditions: C is a curve over a number field K.
conclusion: C(K) is finite.
typical_uses: Identify when high-genus rational point sets are finite.
common_misuses: Applying Faltings to genus 0 or genus 1 curves, where rational points can be infinite.
bridge_lemmas: A Diophantine equation can sometimes be modeled by a smooth projective curve and its genus computed.
repair_templates: Compute or cite the genus before using Faltings; for genus 1 use elliptic-curve methods instead.
